intro_en: In this lesson you will learn to count people and things the Japanese way. Just as Tamil adds a word for people when counting (மூன்று பேர், three people), Japanese has a "counter word" for every kind of thing. You will use counters when shopping, and when saying "how many times" or "how many hours". Along the way you will also learn the small words だけ (மட்டும், only) and ぐらい / ごろ (சுமார், about).

g11-1.explanation_en: When you count things in Japanese, you must add a "counter word" after the number. Tamil adds a counting word for people (பேர், as in மூன்று பேர், three people); Japanese has a word like this for every kind of thing: 〜人 (にん) for people, 〜枚 (まい) for flat things (stamps, paper, photos, plates), 〜台 (だい) for vehicles and machines, 〜本 (ほん) for long cylindrical things (pencils, umbrellas, flowers), 〜匹 (ひき) for small animals, 〜冊 (さつ) for books and notebooks, 〜個 (こ) for small objects, 〜回 (かい) for "times", 〜歳 (さい) for age, and 〜杯 (はい) for cups and glasses. For general things where you don't know which counter to use, you can use 〜つ (ひとつ、ふたつ…). This set only goes up to ten, and its sounds come from the old native Japanese numbers. Note: 一人 (ひとり), 二人 (ふたり) and 二十歳 (はたち) are irregular. With counters like 本, 匹, 杯, 個, 回 and 冊, the sound changes with the numbers 1, 3, 6, 8 and 10 (いっぽん、さんぼん、ろっぽん、はっぽん、じゅっぽん). Read the table below out loud and memorise it.
g11-1.tamil_parallel_en: Three people = 三人 (さんにん); two cups of tea = お茶を二杯. Just as Tamil uses பேர் (people) and கப் (cup) as counting words, Japanese has a counter word for everything.
g11-1.formation_en:
Number + counter
〜つ (general things): ひとつ、ふたつ、みっつ、よっつ、いつつ、むっつ、ななつ、やっつ、ここのつ、とお (question: いくつ)
〜人 (people): ひとり、ふたり、さんにん、よにん、ごにん、ろくにん、しちにん / ななにん、はちにん、きゅうにん、じゅうにん (question: なんにん)
〜枚 (flat things): いちまい、にまい、さんまい、よんまい、ごまい、ろくまい、ななまい、はちまい、きゅうまい、じゅうまい (なんまい)
〜台 (vehicles, machines): いちだい、にだい、さんだい、よんだい、ごだい、ろくだい、ななだい、はちだい、きゅうだい、じゅうだい (なんだい)
〜本 (long things): いっぽん、にほん、さんぼん、よんほん、ごほん、ろっぽん、ななほん、はっぽん、きゅうほん、じゅっぽん (なんぼん)
〜匹 (small animals): いっぴき、にひき、さんびき、よんひき、ごひき、ろっぴき、ななひき、はっぴき、きゅうひき、じゅっぴき (なんびき)
〜冊 (books): いっさつ、にさつ、さんさつ、よんさつ、ごさつ、ろくさつ、ななさつ、はっさつ、きゅうさつ、じゅっさつ (なんさつ)
〜個 (small objects): いっこ、にこ、さんこ、よんこ、ごこ、ろっこ、ななこ、はっこ、きゅうこ、じゅっこ (なんこ)
〜回 (times): いっかい、にかい、さんかい、よんかい、ごかい、ろっかい、ななかい、はっかい、きゅうかい、じゅっかい (なんかい)
〜歳 (age): いっさい、にさい、さんさい、よんさい、ごさい、ろくさい、ななさい、はっさい、きゅうさい、じゅっさい、はたち (20) (なんさい / おいくつ)
〜杯 (cups, glasses): いっぱい、にはい、さんばい、よんはい、ごはい、ろっぱい、ななはい、はっぱい、きゅうはい、じゅっぱい (なんばい)
g11-1.pitfalls_en: A common mistake is to forget the sound changes like いっぽん and さんぼん and say いちほん or さんほん. Only 一人 and 二人 are ひとり and ふたり; from three on it is さんにん, よにん (not よんにん).

g11-2.explanation_en: In Japanese, a quantity (number + counter) usually comes directly before the verb: りんごを三つ買います. The particle を comes after the thing, but no particle comes after the quantity, so you must not say 三つを. This matches the Tamil structure exactly (ஆப்பிளை மூன்று வாங்கினேன், I bought three apples): the object marker (-ஐ) comes after the thing, and the number (மூன்று, three) stands alone before the verb. The same order is used with が and あります / います: 猫が三匹います. If you want to say "a few" or "a lot", you can put 少し or たくさん in this same position.
g11-2.tamil_parallel_en: மிட்டாயை மூன்று வாங்கினேன் ("I bought three sweets") = 飴を三つ買いました. In both languages the quantity stands alone, right before the verb.
g11-2.formation_en:
N + を + [number + counter] + V ます
N + が + [number + counter] + あります / います
g11-2.pitfalls_en: Putting a particle after the quantity, as in 三つを買います or 三人が来ます, is wrong. "Three friends came" = 友達が三人来ました: the quantity goes before the verb.

g11-3.explanation_en: To ask "how many", just put 何 (なん) before the counter: 何人 (なんにん), 何枚 (なんまい), 何台, 何本, 何匹, 何冊, 何個, 何回, 何歳. Only the 〜つ group has its own separate word, いくつ. To ask someone's age politely, you can also say おいくつですか. To ask "how long / how much time", use どのぐらい (or どのくらい). In Tamil, "how many" for countable things (எத்தனை) and "how much" for amounts and time (எவ்வளவு) are different words, and Japanese makes the same distinction: 何 + counter = how many (எத்தனை), どのぐらい = how much / how long (எவ்வளவு). The question word also comes before the verb, in the same place as the quantity.
g11-3.tamil_parallel_en: மாணவர்கள் எத்தனை பேர் இருக்கிறார்கள்? ("How many students are there?") = 学生が何人いますか; எவ்வளவு நேரம்? ("How long?") = どのぐらいですか
g11-3.formation_en:
何 + counter (何人 / 何枚 / 何台 / 何本 / 何匹 / 何冊 / 何個 / 何回 / 何歳)
いくつ (〜つ group; age: おいくつ)
どのぐらい / どのくらい (time, amount)
g11-3.pitfalls_en: いくつ is only for the 〜つ group and for age. Don't ask about people with いくつ; ask 何人. "How much (price)" = いくら (Lesson 3) and "how long" = どのぐらい; don't mix the two up.

g11-4.explanation_en: "At three o'clock" and "for three hours" are different things. In Japanese, 三時 (さんじ) is a point in time (o'clock), while 三時間 (さんじかん) is a length of time (hours); adding 間 (かん) turns it into a duration. In the same way, 一週間 (いっしゅうかん) = one week (duration), 一か月 (いっかげつ) = one month (duration), and 一年 (いちねん) = one year. For days, the same readings used for dates (ふつか、みっか…) are also used for durations; the only difference is "one day" = 一日 (いちにち), while the date "the 1st" is ついたち. Very important: に comes after a point in time (三時に起きます), but に does not come after a length of time (三時間勉強します). Tamil works the same way: "at three o'clock" takes a case ending (மூன்று மணிக்கு, with -க்கு), but "I studied for three hours" has no ending (மூன்று மணி நேரம் படித்தேன்). A length of time also comes before the verb.
g11-4.tamil_parallel_en: மூன்று மணிக்கு எழுந்தேன் ("I got up at three") = 三時に起きました (point in time, with に); மூன்று மணி நேரம் படித்தேன் ("I studied for three hours") = 三時間勉強しました (length of time, no に). Tamil -க்கு behaves just like に here.
g11-4.formation_en:
〜時間 (hours): いちじかん、にじかん、さんじかん、よじかん、ごじかん、ろくじかん、しちじかん、はちじかん、くじかん、じゅうじかん (なんじかん)
〜日 (days): いちにち、ふつか、みっか、よっか、いつか、むいか、なのか、ようか、ここのか、とおか (なんにち)
〜週間 (weeks): いっしゅうかん、にしゅうかん、さんしゅうかん、よんしゅうかん、ごしゅうかん、ろくしゅうかん、ななしゅうかん、はっしゅうかん、きゅうしゅうかん、じゅっしゅうかん (なんしゅうかん)
〜か月 (months): いっかげつ、にかげつ、さんかげつ、よんかげつ、ごかげつ、ろっかげつ、ななかげつ、はっかげつ、きゅうかげつ、じゅっかげつ (なんかげつ)
〜年 (years): いちねん、にねん、さんねん、よねん、ごねん、ろくねん、ななねん、はちねん、きゅうねん、じゅうねん (なんねん)
Length of time + V (no に); question: どのぐらい / 何時間 / 何日 …
g11-4.pitfalls_en: Putting に after a length of time, as in 三時間に勉強します, is wrong; に is only for a point in time. 四時間 = よじかん (not よんじかん), and 九時間 = くじかん.

g11-5.explanation_en: To say "twice a week", put に after the time period and then add 〜回 (かい): 一週間に二回. Here に has the meaning "per" (Tamil -க்கு, as in வாரத்திற்கு, per week). It works with every length of time: 一日に三回 (three times a day), 一か月に一回 (once a month), 一年に二回 (twice a year). To ask, say 一週間に何回 (how many times a week). To say "not even once", use 全然 + a negative (Lesson 9). Like other quantities, 〜回 comes before the verb.
g11-5.tamil_parallel_en: வாரத்திற்கு இரண்டு முறை படம் பார்க்கிறேன் ("I watch a film twice a week") = 一週間に二回映画を見ます. Here に plays the role of Tamil -க்கு ("per").
g11-5.formation_en:
[length of time] + に + [number + 回] + V
一日に / 一週間に / 一か月に / 一年に + 一回、二回、三回 … (question: 何回)
g11-5.pitfalls_en: Don't use で, as in 一週間で二回; for the meaning "per period", it is に. Leaving out に, as in 一週間二回, is also a common mistake.

g11-6.explanation_en: だけ is the direct equivalent of Tamil "only" (மட்டும்). Added after a noun or a quantity, it means "just that, nothing more". After だけ, を or は is usually dropped: コーヒーだけ飲みます ("I drink only coffee"). If you need particles like に or で, you can put them after だけ (日曜日だけ休みます). With quantities: 一つだけ (only one), 二人だけ (only two people). It is just like saying "only one" (ஒன்று மட்டும்) or "only me" (நான் மட்டும்) in Tamil; the position and the meaning are the same.
g11-6.tamil_parallel_en: காபி மட்டும் குடிக்கிறேன் ("I drink only coffee") = コーヒーだけ飲みます; இரண்டு பேர் மட்டும் வந்தார்கள் ("Only two people came") = 二人だけ来ました. だけ sits in the same place as Tamil மட்டும்.
g11-6.formation_en:
N + だけ (+ V): を / は are usually dropped
[number + counter] + だけ
N + だけ + です
g11-6.pitfalls_en: Don't put だけ after the verb (飲みますだけ is wrong). だけ must come directly after the word that "only" refers to.

g11-7.explanation_en: In Tamil, "about" (சுமார்) is the same word whether you say "about three o'clock" or "about three hours". But Japanese has two words. ごろ is only for a point in time (三時ごろ = at about three o'clock, 五月ごろ = around May). ぐらい (or くらい) is for amounts, numbers, lengths of time and prices (三時間ぐらい = about three hours, 十人ぐらい = about ten people, 千円ぐらい = about 1,000 yen). A simple rule: use ごろ after a time that could take に, and ぐらい after a quantity. After ごろ you can drop に (三時ごろ起きます). In questions you will also see どのぐらい, いくつぐらい and 何人ぐらい.
g11-7.tamil_parallel_en: சுமார் மூன்று மணிக்கு ("at about three o'clock") = 三時ごろ (point in time); சுமார் மூன்று மணி நேரம் ("about three hours") = 三時間ぐらい (amount). Tamil uses one word, சுமார், for both, but Japanese splits it.
g11-7.formation_en:
[point in time] + ごろ (に can be dropped)
[number / length of time / price] + ぐらい / くらい
g11-7.pitfalls_en: Using ごろ with an amount, as in 三時間ごろ or 十人ごろ, is wrong; amounts always take ぐらい. You may hear 三時ぐらい in speech, but in the exam write ごろ for a point in time.

items.L11-q01: 切手 = きって (ஸ்டாம்பு, stamp); it has a small っ. きて is the wrong form with the っ missing.
items.L11-q02: 封筒 = ふうとう (envelope); it has two long sounds (ふう, とう). ふとう and ふうと are mistakes with a long sound missing.
items.L11-q03: 二人 is the irregular form ふたり (இரண்டு பேர், two people), not ににん. 〜人 (にん) is only used from three people (さんにん) on.
items.L11-q04: はがき = 葉書 (போஸ்ட் கார்டு, postcard), from 葉 (leaf) + 書 (writing). 菜書 contains the look-alike kanji 菜 (vegetable), so be careful.
items.L11-q05: The counter for books, さつ, is written 冊. 二枚 (にまい) is for flat things; 册 and 卅 are characters that look similar.
items.L11-q06: Books take 〜冊 (さつ). 三本 is for long cylindrical things, and 三枚 is for flat things.
items.L11-q07: To ask how many people, use 何人 (なんにん, எத்தனை பேர், how many people). いくつ is for things and age; we don't use it for people.
items.L11-q08: Cars, machines and similar things take 〜台 (だい). 二匹 is for small animals.
items.L11-q09: 十一時 is a point in time, so "about" is ごろ (சுமார், about). ぐらい is for amounts (十一時間ぐらい).
items.L11-q10: "My younger sister is twenty years old": the age is 二十歳 (はたち, இருபது வயது, twenty years old). The other three are counters for things, times and vehicles.
items.L11-q11: "In the morning I drink only tea": only = だけ (மட்டும்). ずつ (வீதம், each) only goes with a quantity.
items.L11-q12: Twice a week = two days in the week (Monday and Thursday). 一か月に二回 means twice a month, which is a different period.
items.L11-q13: "There is only a cat" means there is no dog. 猫がいません has the opposite meaning; don't mistake だけ (மட்டும், only) for a negative.
items.L11-q14: 三時間ぐらい = about three hours (சுமார் மூன்று மணி நேரம்) = だいたい三時間. 三時ごろ means "at about three o'clock": a point in time, not an amount.
items.L11-q15: A quantity comes alone before the verb, with no particle after it. 切手を already has を, so adding を again in 三枚を is wrong.
items.L11-q16: "Three times a week": after the time period you use に (like Tamil -க்கு, "per"). で is for places and tools; it doesn't fit here.
items.L11-q17: 八時間 is a length of time, so に does not follow it. 八時に (at eight o'clock) needs に, but 時間 (hours) does not.
items.L11-q18: How many people in the family: for people, use 何人 (なんにん, எத்தனை பேர், how many people). いくつ is not used for people.
items.L11-q19: 一時間 is a length of time, so "about" is ぐらい (சுமார், about). ごろ is only for a point in time (一時ごろ).
items.L11-q20: "How many times a year" = 一年に何回 (வருடத்திற்கு எத்தனை முறை). Adding に again, as in 何回に, is wrong; に is already in 一年に.
items.L11-q21: "One postcard each for everyone" = 一枚ずつ (ஒன்று வீதம், one each). ぐらい would mean "about one", which doesn't fit the meaning.
items.L11-q22: 八十円の切手を (80 யென் ஸ்டாம்பை, the 80-yen stamps) → 五枚 (ஐந்து, five) → 買いました. The quantity comes directly before the verb.
items.L11-q23: 一週間に二回 (வாரத்திற்கு இரண்டு முறை, twice a week) → 家族に (குடும்பத்திற்கு, to my family) → 電話をかけます. 〜回 comes right after the time period.
items.L11-q24: 毎晩十一時ごろ (தினமும் இரவு சுமார் 11 மணிக்கு, every night at about 11) → 牛乳を一杯飲みます. ごろ comes after the time, and 一杯 comes before the verb.
items.L11-q25: [1] The younger sister's age = 二十歳 (はたち, இருபது வயது, twenty). [2] A cat is a small animal → 二匹 (இரண்டு, two); 二人 is for people. [3] "Twice a week" is a habit → present tense かけます; かけました is past tense and doesn't fit a habit.
